cards: When a headline says a model is '#1', it usually means a **leaderboard**. The most-cited is the **Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index**, which combines many benchmarks (reasoning, coding, math, knowledge, agentic tasks) into one score. **LMArena** (formerly Chatbot Arena) ranks models by **Elo** from people voting blind on which answer is better.

One combined number hides a lot. A model can lead the index and still be worse at *your* task, or cost 5x more, or be slower. Small gaps (a point or two) are within noise. Indexes also change versions (v4 to v5), so scores across versions don't compare.

Pro move: read the index for *who is in the top tier*, then check the specific sub-benchmarks that match your job (coding, agentic tasks, long context), then check **price and speed**, then run your own evals.
terms: Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index
A composite score combining many benchmarks to rank models' overall intelligence. Widely quoted in launch announcements.
LMArena / Elo
A leaderboard where people vote blind between two models' answers; ratings use the Elo system from chess.
Leaderboard
A ranking of models on one or more benchmarks.
qs: Model A scores 59 on the Intelligence Index, Model B 58. What's the right takeaway?
They're effectively tied; test on your own task
A is clearly smarter at everything
B is useless
Always switch to A
One point on a composite is within noise.
LMArena ranks models using:
Blind human votes turned into Elo ratings
Parameter count
Price
Training data size
Pairwise preference votes, like chess ratings.
You build coding agents. Beyond the headline index, what should you check first?
Agentic coding sub-benchmarks, price, and speed
The model's logo
How many languages it speaks
Its knowledge cutoff only
Match the benchmark to the job.
ex: Explain how to read a 'this model is #1' headline without getting fooled.

It usually means a composite leaderboard like the Artificial Analysis Index or an Elo ranking like LMArena. Treat small gaps as ties, check the sub-benchmarks for your use case plus price and speed, and confirm with your own evals.

cards: The fastest way to make an agent useful is to give it your login. That's also the most dangerous. If an agent signs in with your **credentials**, the service can't tell you from it, and the agent has *all* your power.

The fix is **delegated access**: give the agent its own scoped credential that says who it acts for and what it may do. **OAuth** already works this way. You approve 'read calendar' and the app gets a token for just that, which you can revoke. The industry is now pushing agent-specific versions of this, with identity and audit logs for agents.

Design rules: **least privilege** (only the permissions needed), short-lived tokens, human approval for money or irreversible actions, and logs of everything the agent did. These rules plus prompt-injection defenses are the core of agent security.
terms: Delegated access
Letting an agent act for you using its own limited, revocable permission instead of your full login.
OAuth
Standard for granting an app scoped, revocable access to an account without sharing the password.
Least privilege
Giving a system only the minimum permissions it needs.
Agent identity
Credentials and logs that identify an AI agent separately from the human it acts for.
qs: Why are banks wary of agents using customers' own logins?
The bank can't tell the agent from the person, and it has full account power
Agents type too slowly
Logins expire too fast
It uses too many tokens
No separate identity, no scoping.
Safest way to let an agent pay invoices from your account?
Scoped delegated access plus human approval over a set amount
Give it your password
Give it admin access to everything
Let it only use your password at night
Least privilege plus approval for money.
You approve 'Allow this app to read your calendar.' That's an example of:
OAuth scoped access
Prompt injection
Fine-tuning
A jailbreak
A revocable token limited to one permission.
ex: Why is giving an agent your password a bad idea, and what's the better pattern?

With your password the agent looks exactly like you and can do anything you can, with no limits or clear audit trail. The better pattern is delegated access: a scoped, revocable credential for the agent, least privilege, logging, and human approval for risky actions.

cards: An **API key** is a password for a service. For AI providers, whoever holds your key can run models and you get the bill. That makes AI keys a direct line to expensive compute, so attackers now steal them on purpose. Using stolen keys to run models is called **LLMjacking**.

Keys usually leak from where they're stored: **environment variables** on a hosting platform, code pushed to a public repo, logs, or a breached developer tool. When a platform that holds thousands of customers' keys is breached, every one of those keys is exposed at once.

Defenses: keep keys out of code, give each app its own key with the narrowest **scope**, set **spending caps** and usage alerts at the provider, prefer short-lived credentials, and **rotate** (replace and revoke) keys right away after any suspected leak.
terms: API key
A secret string that lets software call a service on your account.
LLMjacking
Using stolen AI provider credentials to run models on someone else's account and bill.
Environment variable
A setting passed to an app at runtime, often used to hold secrets.
Key rotation
Issuing a new key and revoking the old one so a stolen copy stops working.
Spending cap
A provider-side limit that stops usage once a set amount is spent.
qs: Your hosting platform says all environment variables may have been stolen. First move?
Rotate every key stored there and check provider billing for unusual use
Wait to see if any charges appear
Delete the app
Change your email password only
Assume the keys are compromised: replace and revoke them, then look for abuse.
Why do attackers want AI API keys specifically?
Each key gives free access to costly model usage they can use or resell
Keys reveal the model's weights
Keys let them retrain the model
Keys contain users' chat history
The value is compute on someone else's bill.
Which single control best limits damage if a key leaks?
A spending cap with usage alerts at the provider
A longer key
Storing the key in a code comment
Using the same key for every app
Caps bound the bill; alerts catch abuse fast.
ex: Explain LLMjacking and the three things you'd do to protect an app that uses an AI API.

LLMjacking is when attackers steal AI provider credentials and run models on the victim's account, leaving them the bill. To protect an app: keep the key out of code and give it its own narrowly scoped key, set spending caps and alerts at the provider, and rotate the key immediately after any suspected exposure (and regularly anyway).

cards: AI labs are going public, so their numbers are now in the news. Start with **revenue** and how fast it's growing, then look at **operating income (or loss)**: revenue minus the cost of running the business, including compute, salaries, and research. Operating results tell you whether the core business makes money.

**Net income (or loss)** is the bottom line after everything, including **noncash** accounting items. Fast-rising startups often post giant net losses because **convertible notes** and other instruments are re-valued as the company's value climbs. That's a real accounting entry, but no cash leaves the building, so don't confuse it with burning money.

The other number to watch is **commitments**: contracts to pay for compute, data centers, and leases in future years. They don't show up as losses today, but they are obligations. Compare them with revenue to judge how big a bet the company is making on future demand.
terms: Operating income / loss
Revenue minus the costs of running the business. The best single signal of whether the core business is profitable.
Net income / loss
The final bottom line, including taxes, interest, and noncash accounting items.
Noncash charge
An expense recorded under accounting rules that involves no cash payment, such as re-valuing convertible notes.
Convertible note
A loan to a company that can turn into shares later. Its accounting value rises as the company's valuation rises.
Purchase commitments
Contracts to pay for goods or services, such as compute capacity, in future periods.
qs: A lab reports $17B quarterly revenue, a $0.6B operating loss, and a $23B net loss mostly from re-valuing convertible notes. What's the fairest read?
The core business is near break-even; the big net loss is mostly an accounting effect
The company burned $23B in cash this quarter
The company is about to run out of money
Revenue must have fallen
Operating results show the business; the noncash charge inflates the net loss.
Which number best shows whether an AI lab's core business makes money?
Operating income or loss
Net loss
Total commitments
Valuation
Operating results exclude noncash financing effects.
A company has $895B in compute commitments and about $33B in nine-month revenue. What does that tell you?
It's betting heavily that demand keeps growing for years
It has already spent $895B
It is profitable
Commitments don't matter
Commitments are future obligations, large relative to current revenue.
ex: Explain why an AI lab can post a $100B net loss while its operating loss is around $1B.

Most of the net loss is noncash: accounting rules re-value convertible notes and derivatives as the company's valuation rises, and book the increase as a loss. Operating loss reflects the actual cost of running the business against revenue, so it's the better gauge of how the business itself is doing.

lessons.t: Chip Export Controls and the Cloud Route
cards: The US uses **export controls** to stop the most advanced AI chips (and the tools to make them) from being shipped to China. The theory: training frontier models takes huge amounts of top-end compute, so limiting chips limits capability.

Controls on shipping hardware leave a gap: **remote access**. A company can rent GPU time from a **cloud** in another country and train on the same chips without them ever crossing a border. Closing that gap means checking who the customers are, through **know-your-customer (KYC)** rules, approved-buyer lists, or conditions set by chipmakers themselves.

The other response is **substitution**: building domestic chips like Huawei's Ascend line. They're usually used first for **inference** (running models), which is easier, before **pretraining**, which needs thousands of chips tightly networked. When a lab says it will pretrain on domestic chips, that's the real test of whether controls are working.
terms: Export controls
Government rules restricting the sale or shipment of sensitive technology to certain countries.
Remote access
Using chips over the internet, for example by renting cloud GPUs, instead of owning them.
KYC (know your customer)
Checks a provider does to verify who its customers are and what they're doing.
Substitution
Replacing a restricted product with a domestic alternative, such as Huawei Ascend chips for Nvidia GPUs.
Smuggling / gray market
Controlled chips reaching a banned country through intermediaries, usually at a big markup.
qs: A Chinese AI lab can't buy Nvidia B300s. What's the most common legal-gray way it still trains on them?
Renting cloud GPU time from a data center in another country
Downloading the chip design
Using a VPN on its own servers
Training only on CPUs
Export controls historically restricted shipping hardware, not renting compute abroad.
Why do domestic chips usually get used for inference before training?
Training needs thousands of chips tightly linked for weeks, which is much harder
Inference uses more data
Training doesn't need chips
Inference is illegal on Nvidia
Pretraining stresses chip-to-chip networking and software maturity far more than serving.
A rack sells for ~$600K internationally and ~$2.8M in China. What does that gap signal?
Controls are binding and demand inside China far exceeds legal supply
Chinese chips are better
Nvidia overcharges China on purpose
Shipping costs are high
A large premium means scarcity created by the restrictions.
ex: Explain why a rule saying 51% of a cloud's capacity must go to non-Chinese customers matters for export controls.

Export controls stop chips being shipped to China but not rented abroad, so Chinese labs have trained on foreign clouds. Requiring most capacity to go to non-Chinese customers limits that rental route without needing a new law, though how well it works depends on enforcement and verification.

cards: When you call an AI API, you trust the provider that the model you're paying for is the one answering. Nothing stops a provider, reseller, or router from quietly **swapping** in a cheaper model. **Verifiable inference** is the effort to make that claim checkable.

The main tool is a **zero-knowledge proof** (such as a **zkSNARK**): a short proof that a computation was done correctly, which anyone can verify quickly, without seeing private inputs. The lab publishes a **commitment** (a fingerprint) to its weights; each proof shows the answer came from those exact weights.

The catch is **overhead**: generating proofs for huge models costs many times the compute of just running them (tens of times today). So early uses are **spot-checks** and **audits**, not every chat. Lighter alternatives include signed outputs from trusted hardware and statistical fingerprinting of a model's behavior.
terms: Verifiable inference
Being able to check that a specific model produced a specific output.
Zero-knowledge proof
A proof that something is true that reveals nothing beyond that fact.
zkSNARK
A compact, fast-to-check kind of zero-knowledge proof.
Commitment
A public fingerprint that locks in a set of weights without revealing them.
Proving overhead
The extra compute needed to generate the proof, compared with the original work.
qs: A startup resells 'frontier model' access at a steep discount. What would a provable-inference proof let you check?
That each answer came from the committed frontier model's weights
That the answer is factually correct
That the startup is profitable
That your data wasn't logged
Proofs verify which computation ran, not whether its output is true.
Why can a closed lab use this without leaking its model?
The commitment and proofs reveal nothing about the weights themselves
It uploads weights to a public server
It only works on open models
The weights are encrypted with the user's password
Zero knowledge means the verifier learns only that the claim holds.
If proving costs ~80x the inference compute, what's the realistic first use?
Random spot-checks and audits of high-stakes outputs
Proving every consumer chat
Replacing benchmarks
Speeding up inference
At that overhead, you sample rather than prove everything.
ex: Explain to a friend why 'which model answered me?' is hard to prove, and how a zero-knowledge proof helps.

From outside, an API is a black box: you send text and get text, and a cheaper model can sound similar. A zero-knowledge proof lets the provider attach evidence that the answer was computed with the exact weights it publicly committed to, without revealing those weights. Anyone can check the proof quickly. Today generating the proof is very expensive, so it would be used for spot-checks and audits rather than every request.

cards: "Open weights" only means you can download the model. What you may **do** with it is set by the **license**, and those vary a lot. **Permissive** licenses like **Apache 2.0** and **MIT** let anyone use, change, and sell products built on the model, with little more than keeping the copyright notice.

Many big labs use **custom licenses** that are free for most users but add conditions for large ones. Common patterns: a **revenue or user threshold** above which you need a separate deal, a rule that you must **display the model's name** in your product, limits on **Model as a Service** (reselling raw access via an API), and **acceptable-use** lists of banned purposes.

To read one quickly, ask four questions: Can I use it **commercially**? Is there a **threshold** I could cross? Must I **attribute** it? Am I allowed to **host it for others**? Also check whether the open release matches the API model, since labs sometimes ship different versions.
terms: Permissive license
A license like Apache 2.0 or MIT that allows almost any use, including commercial, with minimal conditions.
Custom model license
A lab-written license with its own conditions, often not approved as open source.
Revenue threshold
A clause that adds obligations once a licensee's revenue or users pass a set level.
Model as a Service
Selling access to the model itself, such as through an API, rather than using it inside your own product.
Attribution requirement
A rule that you must name the model or its maker in your product or documentation.
qs: A startup with $3M in revenue wants to build a chatbot feature on a model whose license requires a separate deal for API resellers above $20M. What applies?
It can use the model freely; it is under the threshold and isn't reselling raw API access
It must pay Moonshot immediately
It cannot use the model commercially at all
It must open-source its whole app
Thresholds only bite when you cross them, and embedding a model in a feature is not Model as a Service.
Which license lets you sell a product built on the model with the fewest conditions?
Apache 2.0
A custom license with a 100M-user display rule
A research-only license
A non-commercial license
Apache 2.0 is permissive: keep the notices and you can sell.
A cloud provider with billions in revenue wants to offer an open model through its API under a license with a $20M Model-as-a-Service clause. What should it do first?
Sign the separate agreement with the model's maker
Nothing, open weights mean anything goes
Rename the model
Only offer it for free
Large resellers are exactly who these clauses target.
ex: Explain why 'open weights' doesn't automatically mean you can do anything with a model.

Open weights means the files are downloadable, but a license still governs use. Permissive ones like Apache 2.0 allow nearly anything. Custom ones can require a separate deal above a revenue or user threshold, force you to display the model's name, or limit reselling API access. So you check commercial use, thresholds, attribution, and hosting rights before building on it.

cards: A software **vulnerability** is a bug an attacker can use. Finding one is only step one. The full chain is **find** the suspicious code, **reproduce** it (prove it really crashes or misbehaves), **exploit** it (show it gives an attacker real power, like **root**), **patch** it, and **disclose** it to the maintainers.

AI agents now run that chain at scale. Labs split it into stages: cheap agents narrow the code to what's reachable, others propose bugs, a test harness confirms them in isolated machines, and stronger models write exploits and fixes. The cost per bug falls to hundreds or thousands of dollars, versus tens of thousands in **bug bounties**.

The bottleneck moves to humans. Maintainers must review, prioritize, and ship fixes, and **coordinated disclosure** (private report, time to patch, then publish) assumes a trickle, not a flood. The same tools in attackers' hands shrink the time between a bug landing and a working exploit, so **patch speed** and **sandboxing** matter more.
terms: Privilege escalation
Turning limited access (a normal user or sandboxed app) into higher access, usually administrator or root.
Exploit
Working code that uses a vulnerability to do something the attacker shouldn't be able to do.
Coordinated disclosure
Reporting a bug privately to maintainers and publishing only after they've had time to fix it.
CVE
A public ID number for a specific known vulnerability, used to track fixes across vendors.
Sandbox
An isolated environment that limits what code can touch if it misbehaves or is compromised.
qs: An AI pipeline reports 2,000 possible kernel bugs. What should happen before any are reported to maintainers?
Reproduce them in isolated test machines and have humans review the results
Publish them all immediately so everyone can patch
Assume they're all real and file CVEs
Ignore them because AI findings are unreliable
Reproduction filters false positives, and human review keeps maintainers from being buried in noise.
Why does a local privilege escalation bug matter if an attacker already has a normal account?
It turns a small foothold into full control of the machine
It doesn't; they already have access
It only matters on phones
It lets them log in remotely without a password
Most real attacks chain a foothold with an escalation to get admin rights.
If AI makes finding exploits cheap for everyone, which defense gains the most value?
Patching quickly and sandboxing untrusted code
Keeping source code secret
Switching to a different programming language overnight
Turning off logging
Cheap discovery shortens the window between bug and exploit, so fast updates and containment matter most.
ex: Explain why AI that finds bugs cheaply is both good and bad news for defenders.

Good: defenders can find and fix far more bugs before attackers do, at a fraction of bounty prices. Bad: attackers get the same ability, and maintainers can't review and patch hundreds of reports at once. The bottleneck shifts from finding bugs to validating, prioritizing, and shipping fixes, so patch speed and sandboxing become the main defenses.

cards: **State tracking** is keeping a correct, current picture of something that changes over a sequence: a variable's value after many reassignments, a game board after many moves, or which files an agent has already edited. It's different from **retrieval**, which is just finding a fact somewhere in the text.

**Transformers** look back over the whole input with attention at every step. That's great for retrieval, but they have no built-in running memory, so long chains of updates can trip them up even inside a huge **context window**. **Recurrent** designs (like **Gated DeltaNet** or state space models) carry a fixed-size memory forward and update it at each step, which suits tracking change.

Many new models are **hybrids** that mix attention layers with recurrent layers to get both. In practice today, the reliable fix is to let the model offload state to **tools**: code, a scratchpad file, or a database it updates and reads back.
terms: State tracking
Following how values or situations change across a sequence and knowing the current state.
Recurrent model
A model that processes input step by step and carries a running memory forward.
Gated DeltaNet
A recurrent-style architecture with a fixed-size memory that it selectively updates each step.
Hybrid architecture
A model mixing attention layers with recurrent or state space layers.
Length generalization
Working correctly on inputs longer than any seen in training.
qs: You paste a 50,000-line change log into a chatbot and ask for each setting's final value. What's the most reliable approach?
Have the model write and run code that replays the log
Trust the answer because the log fits in the context window
Ask the model to think harder
Split the log and only send the last page
Fitting in context doesn't guarantee every update is applied; code tracks state exactly.
Which task is retrieval rather than state tracking?
Finding the sentence that names the CEO
Knowing x's value after 1,000 reassignments
Knowing a chess position after 80 moves
Knowing which files an agent already changed
Retrieval finds a fixed fact; the others require applying changes in order.
Why might a recurrent model trained on a tracking task generalize to inputs 10x longer?
It updates a running memory each step, so length doesn't change the procedure
It has a bigger context window
It memorized the test set
Recurrent models always beat transformers
Applying the same update rule step by step works at any length, if the memory holds what's needed.
ex: Explain why a model with a million-token context window can still get 'what's the current value?' questions wrong.

Seeing all the text isn't the same as correctly applying every change in order. Transformers re-read the input with attention rather than keeping a running memory, so long chains of updates get muddled. Recurrent or hybrid designs carry state forward and do better, and in practice you can have the model track state with code or a scratchpad.

cards: When a lab trains a model to refuse harmful requests, that refusal lives in the model's **weights**. Researchers found that refusal often runs through a single direction inside the model's internal activations. **Abliteration** finds that direction and edits the weights to remove it, so the model stops refusing, with no retraining.

This only works on **open-weight** models, because you need the weights to edit them. With a closed **API** model, the provider keeps the weights and can add outside filters, monitoring, and account bans. That is why safeguards on commercial APIs held up in real attack cases while attackers simply ran stripped open models locally.

Abliteration usually costs some capability: the edited model makes more mistakes. The policy debate is whether the benefits of open weights (research, privacy, competition, local control) outweigh the fact that **safeguards can be removed** once weights are public. Defenders should assume capable, unfiltered models are available to attackers.
terms: Abliteration
Editing a model's weights to remove its refusal behavior without retraining.
Refusal direction
A pattern in a model's internal activations that tends to trigger refusals.
Open weights
A model whose trained parameters are downloadable, so anyone can run or modify it.
API safeguards
Protections a provider adds around a hosted model: filters, monitoring, rate limits, bans.
qs: An attacker's requests are refused by every commercial API they try. What is the most likely next move?
Run an abliterated open-weight model on their own GPUs
Ask the API politely in another language forever
Give up, since all models refuse
Wait for the API provider to approve them
Open weights can be edited to remove refusals, and nobody can monitor local use.
Why can't someone abliterate a model they only reach through an API?
They don't have the weights to edit
APIs have no refusals
Abliteration needs internet access
APIs are too slow
Abliteration modifies weights directly, which an API user never sees.
What is a typical cost of abliterating a model?
It often becomes less accurate and makes more errors
It becomes much smarter
It loses the ability to write code entirely
It can only answer in English
Editing internals is blunt; capability usually drops somewhat.
ex: Explain why safety training on an open-weight model is weaker protection than on an API model.

Once weights are public, anyone can modify them. Techniques like abliteration remove the refusal behavior directly, and no one can watch how the local copy is used. An API provider keeps the weights and can layer on filters, monitoring, and bans, so its safeguards are much harder to strip away.

lessons.t: Who Pays for a Data Center's Power
cards: A big AI data center can draw hundreds of megawatts, as much as a small city. Serving it can require new **transmission lines, substations, and power plants**. Utilities normally recover such costs from all customers through rates, so households can end up paying for upgrades built for one company.

A **large-load tariff** is a special electricity rate that makes very big users pay the costs they cause, often with long contracts and **financial guarantees** so others aren't stuck with the bill if the project shrinks or is canceled. **Demand flexibility** (or curtailment) means the data center agrees to cut usage, or switch to batteries or on-site generation, when the grid is strained.

These levers matter because local opposition, driven by electricity bills, water, and noise, is now a real limit on AI buildout. The cost and speed of getting power connected shape where data centers get built, how fast labs get compute, and ultimately what AI services cost.
terms: Large-load tariff
An electricity rate for very large customers that charges them the grid costs they create.
Curtailment
Reducing a customer's power use on request when the grid is under stress.
Interconnection
Getting a new user or power plant hooked up to the grid, often a multi-year queue.
Ratepayers
The utility's customers, whose bills fund grid costs.
qs: A town worries a new data center will raise household power bills. Which policy most directly addresses that?
A large-load tariff that charges the data center its own grid costs
A tax on electric cars
Banning all new homes
Lowering the data center's rate
It assigns the upgrade costs to the customer that needs them.
Why would a data center agree to curtailment?
To get connected faster or more cheaply by easing peak grid demand
Because AI chips need less power at night
It's required by all federal law
To increase its electricity bill
Agreeing to cut use at peaks reduces the new capacity the grid must build.
Why do chip stocks fall when towns vote to limit data centers?
Fewer or slower data centers mean fewer chip orders
Chips are made in those towns
Voters own chip stocks
Data centers don't use chips
Chip sales depend on new buildings filling with servers.
ex: Explain why a data center's power hookup can become a cost for ordinary households, and one way to prevent that.

Serving a huge new load can require new lines, substations, and generation, and utilities usually spread those costs across all ratepayers. A large-load tariff with long contracts and financial guarantees makes the data center pay for what it needs, and demand-flexibility agreements reduce how much new capacity has to be built at all.

lessons.t: When AI Speeds Up AI Research
cards: Frontier labs now use their own models to write code, run experiments, and analyze results. If that help is big enough, each new model arrives faster than the last. This is **AI R&D acceleration**, and the extreme version is a feedback loop sometimes called **recursive self-improvement**.

To measure it, evaluators track a **capability index** (many benchmark scores combined into one number) over time and look for a **trend break**: a point where the slope gets steeper. Then comes the hard part, **attribution**: how much of the speedup came from AI help versus more compute, more staff, or better ideas. Interviews, usage data, and compute records all feed in, and the uncertainty is wide.

Labs tie this to safety rules. Anthropic's policy, for example, has a **2x acceleration threshold** that triggers stronger safeguards. Because the lab grades itself and can redact evidence, **independent assessments** by outside groups like METR matter, but only as much as the access they get.
terms: AI R&D acceleration
AI tools speeding up the work of building the next AI model.
Capability index
A single score combining many benchmarks to track overall progress.
Trend break
The point where a progress curve changes slope.
Attribution
Estimating how much of a change is due to a specific cause, here AI help.
Independent assessment
An outside evaluator reviewing a lab's claims with some inside access.
qs: A lab's capability index rose 15 points a year, then 29 points a year after a certain date. What has it most likely measured?
A trend break showing roughly 2x faster progress
Proof that AI built the model alone
A drop in compute use
A benchmark error
Nearly doubling the slope is about a 2x acceleration; it says nothing yet about the cause.
Progress doubled, but the lab also tripled its training compute in the same period. What should an evaluator do before blaming AI help?
Separate out the compute effect before attributing the speedup
Assume AI caused all of it
Ignore compute because benchmarks don't measure it
Stop measuring
Attribution means ruling out other causes like more compute.
Why does it matter that a lab can redact an outside evaluator's report?
The public can't check the strongest evidence behind the conclusions
Redaction makes the numbers more accurate
Redaction is illegal
It means the lab crossed its threshold
Independent review is only as checkable as what gets published.
ex: Explain how you would tell whether AI is really speeding up a lab's AI research.

Track a combined capability score over time and look for a lasting increase in its slope. Then rule out other causes, like more compute or staff, using compute records and interviews, and estimate what share is left for AI help. Compare against other labs' progress to check the baseline, and have an outside evaluator with real access verify it, since the lab is grading itself.

cards: A company going public files an **S-1** with the SEC, then sets a **price range** per share. Over a one to two week **roadshow**, it and its bankers pitch large investors, who place orders saying how many shares they want and at what price. This process is called **book building**, and the list of orders is **the book**.

At **pricing**, the night before trading starts, the bankers set the final price from the book. If demand is strong (the book is **oversubscribed**), the price can go above the range; if weak, below it, or the deal is delayed. Companies usually leave an **IPO discount** so the stock rises on day one, which keeps big buyers happy for future deals.

Private valuations and public prices are different things. A private round sets a price for a few investors; an IPO needs thousands of buyers at once, priced against similar public stocks that day. That is why a market selloff can cut an IPO's valuation by hundreds of billions without anything changing inside the company.
terms: The registration filing with financials and risks a company files before an IPO.
Roadshow
The pre-IPO tour of investor meetings that gathers orders.
Book building
Collecting investor orders to discover what price the market will pay.
Oversubscribed
More shares ordered than are being sold.
IPO discount
Pricing below expected trading value so the stock is likely to rise on day one.
Lockup
A period, often 180 days, when insiders cannot sell their shares after the IPO.
qs: A company's private round valued it at $1 trillion. During its roadshow the book is thin. What is most likely?
It prices at or below its range, or delays the deal
It must price at $1 trillion because of the private round
The SEC sets a higher price to protect early investors
The IPO proceeds at the top of the range anyway
Public pricing comes from the orders in the book that week, not from past private rounds.
Why do companies often price an IPO a bit below what they think it is worth?
To leave a first-day gain that rewards buyers and supports future demand
Because the SEC caps IPO prices
To reduce the number of shares sold
Because private investors require it in the S-1
A modest discount keeps institutions willing to buy this and future deals.
Investors say a company's October revenue is blank in its updated S-1. Why would they care before pricing?
It is the most recent sign of whether growth is slowing, which drives the price they will pay
Blank fields make the IPO illegal
Revenue does not affect IPO pricing
It means the company has no revenue
Buyers price growth; the newest month tells them the most about the current trend.
ex: Explain why an AI company's IPO valuation could fall 25% in a month without its business changing.

An IPO is priced by what public buyers will pay at that moment, through book building during the roadshow. Those buyers compare the company to similar public stocks. If AI stocks fall sharply, comparable valuations drop, investors demand a bigger discount, and the price that clears the book falls, even if the company's revenue and products are unchanged.

cards: A **proof assistant** such as **Lean** lets you write a math proof as code. A small trusted program, the **kernel**, checks that every step follows from the previous ones by the rules of logic. If the proof compiles with no gaps (no **sorry** placeholders or extra **axioms**), the steps are valid, no matter who or what wrote them.

That matters for AI because language models can write convincing nonsense. A human referee might miss a subtle error in 40 pages; Lean will not. So AI math claims backed by a Lean check are much stronger than claims backed only by the model's own explanation, and labs increasingly pair models with Lean to search for proofs.

The check has a limit: Lean proves the **formal statement** you gave it. If that statement does not match the real problem (a missing condition, a slightly different definition), the proof is valid but answers the wrong question. That is why experts still read the formal statement and the argument, and why outside review still counts.
terms: Proof assistant
Software that checks each step of a proof written in a formal language.
Lean
A widely used proof assistant and programming language with a large math library, Mathlib.
Kernel
The small core of a proof assistant that does the actual checking and must be trusted.
Formalization
Translating a math statement and proof into a proof assistant's language.
Axiom
A statement accepted without proof; adding new ones can make anything provable.
Autoformalization
Using AI to translate ordinary math into formal code automatically.
qs: A lab says its model proved a famous conjecture and the Lean proof compiles with no placeholders. What is the main thing experts still need to check?
That the formal statement actually matches the real conjecture
Whether Lean made an arithmetic mistake
Whether the model was large enough
How long the run took
Lean verifies the proof of the statement as written; a mismatched statement means a valid proof of the wrong thing.
Why are Lean-checked AI proofs more trustworthy than a model's written explanation?
Every logical step is mechanically verified by a small trusted checker
Lean only accepts proofs written by humans
Lean runs the model a second time to compare
Lean checks whether the result is famous
The kernel checks each step, so persuasive but wrong reasoning cannot pass.
A formal proof compiles, but the authors added a new axiom stating a key lemma is true. How should you read it?
The result now depends on that unproven assumption
It is fully proved because it compiled
Axioms are always safe to add
Lean rejects any added axioms automatically
An added axiom is assumed, not proved, so the proof is only as good as that assumption.
ex: Explain why a Lean-verified AI proof can still be wrong about the problem it claims to solve.

Lean checks that each step is valid for the exact formal statement written in code. If humans or the AI formalized the problem slightly wrong, with a missing condition or a different definition, the proof is correct for that statement but does not settle the real question. Experts must still confirm the formal statement matches the intended problem.

cards: Models are stateless, so an agent 'remembers' only what gets written down and fed back in. Agent memory usually has layers: raw **transcripts** of past work, **notes** the agent writes, larger **representations** like wikis built from those notes, and a small block of **injected context** loaded into every session. Each layer up is smaller and more useful, but further from the original evidence.

The hard part is **salience**: deciding what to save before you know what will matter. Save too much and memory fills with stale or contradictory notes the agent has to wade through. Save too little and it repeats mistakes. Stronger models tend to save less but better, such as tested rules and plans rather than facts they can see again anyway.

**Consolidation** (Anthropic calls it **dreaming**; researchers call it **sleep-time compute**) is a background pass that rereads transcripts while the agent is idle, fixes wrong notes, and reorganizes them. It catches errors the agent made in the moment, at the cost of extra compute and a delay before the improved memory is available.
terms: Agent memory
Knowledge an agent keeps across sessions as stored text, not as changes to model weights.
Salience
How much a piece of information will matter later; agents must guess it when saving.
Consolidation / dreaming
An offline pass that reviews logs, corrects notes, and builds better summaries.
Sleep-time compute
Using idle time to process past experience so future sessions start smarter.
Injected context
The small, always-loaded memory and instructions at the start of every session.
qs: Your agent's memory folder has grown to hundreds of files and its performance is slipping. What is the most likely cause?
Stale and redundant notes are crowding out what matters
The model's weights are degrading
Too few tokens in the context window
Memory files slow the GPU
More saved notes is not better; stale memory misleads and distracts the agent.
An agent wrote a wrong note mid-task and keeps acting on it. Which approach is designed to fix this?
A background pass that checks notes against transcripts and corrects them
Restarting the model with a higher temperature
Deleting all transcripts
Adding more instructions to the system prompt
Consolidation compares notes with the raw record and repairs errors the agent made in the moment.
You add a strict rule, 'only save failures,' to a strong model's memory instructions. What did Anthropic's tests suggest?
It cost the model much of its memory gain
It always improves results
It has no effect
It makes the model forget its training
Strong models did better with general guidance; rigid save rules removed useful memories.
ex: Explain why an AI agent's memory can make it worse, and what consolidation does about it.

An agent saves notes before it knows what will matter, so memory accumulates stale, wrong, or redundant entries that mislead it later. Consolidation runs in the background, rereads the original transcripts, corrects bad notes, and reorganizes the rest, so future sessions start from cleaner, more accurate memory. It costs extra compute and adds delay.

lessons.t: Copyright vs. Voice Rights in AI
cards: AI companies face two different legal claims, and they work differently. **Copyright** protects specific works: a song's lyrics and melody, a recording, a book. Claims are about copying, either during **training** (making copies of works to learn from) or in **outputs** (spitting out something too close to the original). The main defense for training is **fair use**, which courts are still deciding case by case.

The **right of publicity** protects a person's identity: name, likeness, and in some states, voice. It doesn't care whether any specific work was copied. A model that never reproduces a single song can still violate it by generating a convincing imitation of a particular singer. Laws vary by state; Tennessee's **ELVIS Act** (2024) explicitly covers AI simulations of a voice.

In practice, **verbatim output** is the weakest spot for AI companies, because reproducing lyrics or text word for word is hard to call transformative. Publicity claims are a second front that doesn't depend on how fair use is resolved. That is why voice-cloning and 'in the style of' features carry legal risk even if training itself is eventually ruled legal.
terms: Copyright
Legal protection for a specific creative work against unauthorized copying.
Fair use
A US defense allowing some unlicensed use, judged on purpose, amount, and market harm.
Right of publicity
A person's right to control commercial use of their name, likeness, and voice.
ELVIS Act
Tennessee's 2024 law adding voice, including AI imitations, to publicity rights.
Verbatim output
A model reproducing source text or lyrics word for word.
qs: An AI music app never outputs any real song but lets users make tracks that sound exactly like a famous singer. Which claim fits best?
Right of publicity
Copyright infringement of a specific song
Patent infringement
Trademark dilution
Imitating a person's voice targets their identity, which publicity law protects, even if no work is copied.
Which fact would most hurt an AI company's fair use defense?
Its model outputs a song's lyrics word for word
It trained on public web pages
It charges a subscription
It uses a transformer architecture
Verbatim reproduction looks like copying, not transformation, and can substitute for the original.
A court rules that training on copyrighted songs is fair use. Are voice-imitation claims over?
No, publicity rights are a separate claim
Yes, fair use covers every claim
Yes, but only in Tennessee
No, but only for living artists
Publicity rights protect identity, not works, so a fair use ruling on training doesn't decide them.
ex: Explain the difference between suing an AI company for copyright and for right of publicity.

Copyright protects specific works, so the claim is that the company copied songs or text, in training or in outputs; the main defense is fair use. Right of publicity protects a person's identity, like their voice, so the claim is that the model imitates the artist, even without copying any work. The two are independent, so winning on fair use doesn't end a voice-imitation suit.

cards: Big AI models don't run on one chip. They are split across many, and the chips constantly trade data. So a system's speed depends on the **accelerators** (the chips doing the math) and on the **interconnect** (the wiring between them). A fast chip on a slow link sits idle waiting for data.

There are two layers of wiring. **Scale-up** links connect chips inside a rack so tightly they act like one big chip; Nvidia's **NVLink** is the best-known. **Scale-out** networks (InfiniBand or Ethernet) connect racks to each other and are slower. Nvidia's lead comes partly from owning both, not just the GPU.

Not every chip is a GPU. An **NPU** or other **ASIC** is built only for AI math, often for **inference**, and can be cheaper per answer but less flexible. Programs like **NVLink Fusion** let other companies' chips join Nvidia's scale-up fabric, so customers can mix chips while still buying Nvidia's racks and networking.
terms: Accelerator
A chip specialized for the math AI needs, like a GPU or NPU.
Interconnect
The links that move data between chips; often the real bottleneck.
Scale-up
Tightly linking chips within a rack so they behave like one.
Scale-out
Networking many racks together, at lower bandwidth.
NPU / ASIC
A custom chip built for one job, such as running AI models.
qs: A company doubles its chips' raw math speed but keeps the same links between them. Training barely speeds up. Most likely why?
The chips are waiting on data over the interconnect
The model is too small to train
GPUs can't run training
The software has a memory leak
When chips trade data constantly, a slow link leaves the faster chips idle.
Why would Nvidia let a rival's inference chip connect to its NVLink?
So customers mixing chips still buy Nvidia racks and networking
Because NVLink is a free public standard
To make its GPUs slower
Regulators require it everywhere
Opening the link keeps Nvidia in the system even when some chips aren't Nvidia's.
Which job is a specialized NPU usually best suited for?
Running a finished model cheaply at high volume
Researching brand-new model architectures
Rendering video games
Storing training data
NPUs trade flexibility for efficiency on known workloads like inference.
ex: Explain why the links between AI chips matter as much as the chips.

Large models are split across many chips that must constantly exchange data. If the links are slow, the chips wait, so the whole system runs at the speed of the interconnect. That is why scale-up links like NVLink, which make a rack of chips act like one, are a big part of Nvidia's advantage, and why opening them to other chips (NVLink Fusion) matters.
